newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: HOWARD SAYS NO DECISION ON GST REFERENDUM
Prime Minister John Howard says there's nothing wrong with ministers raising options in the debate over taxation, but no decision has been made to hold a plebiscite on a Goods and Services Tax.
Howard says the idea, raised by Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith, is just one of many options.
He says Australia has to honestly address the problems in the taxation system, and he's prepared to lead a constructive debate.

Howard says Government's can't win because they're bucketed for lacking courage and guts when they won't discuss anything openly and bucketed for openess when they do discuss something. He says the important thing is to get a better tax system in Australia, not to have a series of debating checkmates along the path.
AUST COULD BECOME BASE FOR FIGHTER JET MAINTENANCE
Australia could become the maintenance base for fighter jet trainers sold in the Asia-Pacific region, under a deal to assemble 21 Hawk trainers in the New South Wales city of Newcastle.
The contract, to be signed tomorrow, is worth nearly $1 billion and will see British Aerospace supply 33 Hawke trainers to the Airforce.
The Prime Minister says around 300 jobs will be created in Newcastle and states such as Western Australia and Victoria during the 25-year life of the project.
The first 12 planes built in the UK will be delivered to Australia by the year 2000, and the on-going maintenance and support will be done in Australia.
Howard says the project will bring jobs, hope and optimism to Newcastle.
British Aerospace Chief Executive Sir Richard Evans says the base in Australia will be part of the sales pitch for the plane in the rest of the region.
LATEST GROUP OF BOAT PEOPLE WELL ORGANISED AND FUNDED
The Federal Immigration Minister says it appears the 139 boat people who arrived in Torres Strait more than a week ago were well organised and spent lot of money to get to Australia.
The group was apprehended when its boat became stranded on a sand bar off Thursday Island.
They were transferred to the Port Hedland Detention Centre, where it was established their voyage began in China's Fujian Provence.
Immigration Minister, Philip Ruddock says it is too early for a decision on the fate of the group.
He says detailed interviews with the detainees are continuing, and arrangements for their future will be undertaken in concert with the Chinese Government.
BIG WEEK IN PARLIAMENT BEFORE WINTER RECESS
Debate on the Federal Government's controversial work-for-the-dole scheme resumes in the Senate today.
With a week left before Parliament winds up for winter recess, the scheme, along with the planned Constitutional Convention will be high on the week's political agenda.
The work-for-dole bill is facing significant changes in the Senate, with the Upper House poised to reject the program's compulsory aspects.
But the Government has warned that could eventually provide a trigger for a double dissolution election.
On the Convention, the non-Government parties in the Senate are expected to once again insist on a compulsory direct vote for delegates.
But the Government says that could jeopardise the event and de-rail any push towards a Republic.
And the ALP is also set to continue its pursuit of Small Business Minister Geoff Prosser over his various business interests.
JABILUKA TRADITIONAL OWNERS TAKE CASE TO PARIS
Traditional owners of the proposed Jabiluka uranium mine site, alongside the Northern Territory's Kakadu National Park, have lodged a submission with the World Heritage Bureau in Paris.
Spokesperson Jacqui Katona says the submission seeks an "under threat" listing, in recognition of the threat that further mining would pose to the area's cultural values.
She says after 20 years of mining in Kakadu National Park, it's clear that the culture of Aboriginal people has been affected by uranium mining.
Katona says it's not an issue of money, but an issue of welfare and of a society's culture being significantly disadvantaged by uranium mining.
SEARCH RESUMES AFTER SEVERED HEAD FOUND
Police will resume a search today for clues to the murder of a man whose severed head was discovered in Sydney's south over the weekend.
A man and a woman walking in Gough Whitlam Park, at Tempe, yesterday, spotted a black carry bag on the banks of the Cooks River.
Inside was a severed human head, wrapped in a white sheet.
Police divers will search the Cooks River today while other officers will continue to scour the park.
